title: Collection and transfer of a biological sample for storage enables disclosure of sensitive biological data
description: Sending a physical biological sample from the wet lab to storage constitutes handling and continued collection/use of highly sensitive material that can reveal health, genetic, or other intimate characteristics of the data subject beyond the immediate operational need if not strictly governed.
assumptions: Assumes the physical sample is human-derived or otherwise linked to an identifiable or reasonably linkable data subject.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC PA03.11 clearly fits biological sample handling, but the exact LINDDUN tree-node mapping is best-effort because the flow concerns transfer for storage rather than initial collection from the subject.

title: Stored biological sample may enable broader processing or secondary use than expected
description: On receipt into physical sample storage, the retained specimen can be preserved for future testing, extraction, or reuse, creating a risk that more personal information is derived or disclosed later than the data subject expects or than was originally necessary.
assumptions: Assumes the storage facility retains samples over time and that stored specimens remain accessible for future analysis or sharing.
uncertainty_note: This is grounded in the sensitivity and reusability of biological samples under PA03.11; the threat is about downstream disclosure from storage rather than the transit event itself.

title: Persistent sample storage increases linkability of the specimen to the individual across contexts
description: Retaining the physical sample in organized freezer storage can allow the specimen to be linked back to the same individual across studies, datasets, or future analyses, especially where identifiers, labels, or custody metadata accompany the sample.
assumptions: Assumes samples are labeled or otherwise associated with identifiers, codes, or chain-of-custody metadata.
uncertainty_note: PA03.11 is applicable because the object is a biological sample; linkability arises mainly from storage practices and associated metadata, not necessarily from the mere physical movement.

title: De-identified sample ID may still permit re-identification
description: LIMS sends a de-identified ID back to the wet lab for sample use, but if the identifier is pseudonymous, stable across contexts, or derivable from internal mappings, the sample metadata may be insufficiently de-identified. This can enable the wet lab or anyone with auxiliary knowledge to reconnect the sample to an individual.
assumptions: Assumes the returned ID is not fully anonymized and that the wet lab may have access to contextual or operational information that could support re-identification.
uncertainty_note: PA06.07 is a strong fit if the 'de-identified ID' is actually pseudonymous or otherwise reversible/linkable; if the identifier is one-time and non-linkable, this threat may be reduced.

title: Returned de-identified ID can enable linkage of sample records
description: On receipt, the wet lab may use the de-identified ID as a persistent key to join sample metadata with other laboratory, operational, or study records. Even without direct identifiers in this flow, the identifier can facilitate linking records about the same subject or specimen across datasets.
assumptions: Assumes the wet lab stores or can access additional records keyed by the same or correlatable identifier.
uncertainty_note: The PANOPTIC match is approximate here: PA06.07 directly concerns insufficient de-identification, while the concrete privacy effect at the destination is linkability through reuse of the identifier.

title: Stored raw sequence data can disclose sensitive subject characteristics
description: The cluster filesystem receives and stores digital raw sequence data. Genomic raw data inherently contains highly sensitive information about an individual and potentially relatives; persisting it at the destination creates a privacy threat of disclosure if the stored artifact is accessible beyond the intended need or later reused.
assumptions: Assumes the sequence data is human or otherwise attributable to a data subject and is stored in identifiable or potentially identifiable form.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 Recording is the closest retrieved PANOPTIC activity because the destination is creating/persisting a digital artifact. The exact PANOPTIC sub-activity for storage/retention may differ if a more specific taxonomy entry exists.

title: Raw sequence data may be insufficiently de-identified when stored
description: If the sequence data is stored without adequate de-identification or with residual identifiers, the destination's storage of the dataset may enable singling out or later attribution of the data subject from the genomic content itself.
assumptions: Assumes the dataset is intended to be de-identified, pseudonymized, or otherwise handled as privacy-protected data, but genomic data remains inherently identifying or quasi-identifying.
uncertainty_note: This applies strongly to human genomic data because sequence data can itself be identifying; if the data is fully non-human or otherwise out of scope for personal data, this threat may not apply.

title: Stored sequence data can support re-identification
description: Once raw sequence data is stored in the cluster filesystem, it may be matched with other datasets or metadata to re-associate the data with a specific individual, even if direct identifiers were removed before transfer.
assumptions: Assumes auxiliary datasets, metadata, or future analytical capability exist that could be used to link the stored sequence data back to a person.
uncertainty_note: Re-identification is a well-known risk for genomic data, but applicability depends on whether the sequence data concerns identifiable humans and what auxiliary data is available.

title: Compute nodes record and retain raw sequence data during processing
description: On receipt of raw digital sequence data, the compute nodes may create local copies, caches, logs, checkpoints, or temporary files as part of transformation workflows. Because sequence data can be highly sensitive and potentially identifying, this recording/retention at the destination increases the risk of privacy disclosure beyond the original transfer purpose.
assumptions: Compute workflows may materialize input data in scratch space, memory dumps, logs, or intermediate artifacts rather than processing purely in-stream.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 'Recording' is a best-fit PANOPTIC activity from the retrieved context; the exact PANOPTIC sub-activity for computational reuse/temporary replication may differ.

title: Compute nodes can profile or link subjects from raw sequence data
description: Raw sequence data received by the compute nodes may be analyzed together with other available datasets, metadata, or prior runs to assemble subject-specific profiles or link records to individuals or cohorts. This creates a linkability risk at the destination because the recipient's processing can organize and correlate highly distinctive genomic information.
assumptions: The compute environment or downstream jobs have access to metadata, reference datasets, or prior outputs that enable correlation or subject-level organization.
uncertainty_note: PA08.01 is applicable if the compute processing organizes or correlates sequence data about subjects; if the workflow is strictly one-off transformation without correlation, this threat may be less applicable.

title: Compute processing may infer subject identity or sensitive attributes from sequence data
description: Even if the transferred data is not explicitly labeled with direct identifiers, the compute nodes can process raw sequence data to infer identity, kinship, ancestry, disease predispositions, or other sensitive characteristics. The destination's receipt and analysis therefore creates an identifiability risk.
assumptions: The sequence data is sufficiently rich to support re-identification or sensitive inference, which is commonly true for genomic raw data.
uncertainty_note: The PANOPTIC mapping is approximate: PA08.01 'Profiling' best captures analytic organization/inference here, though identifiability may also map to a different PANOPTIC activity not present in the retrieved context.

title: Making research data available in the delivery DMZ beyond its justified lifecycle or audience
description: The source datastore shares context-relevant research data into a delivery DMZ specifically to make it available for delivery. This can create a disclosure threat if data that should no longer be exposed, or should remain confined to a narrower environment, is afforded for access in the DMZ beyond the end of its legitimate lifecycle or beyond the intended recipient set.
assumptions: Assumes the delivery DMZ is less restricted or more broadly reachable than the cluster filesystem environment, and that lifecycle, retention, or audience constraints apply to at least some of the research data being transferred.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC match PA10.01 is a strong semantic fit because the flow explicitly makes data available for delivery, but the exact lifecycle status of the data is not stated.

title: Receiving or staging research data in the DMZ that is out of scope for delivery
description: On receipt, the destination datastore may hold data types or fields that exceed what is permitted or necessary for the delivery purpose. If the DMZ stores broader context-relevant research data than authorized for this delivery channel, the action creates an unnecessary disclosure surface and violates scope limits.
assumptions: Assumes there are purpose, policy, contractual, or legal limits on which research data elements may be staged in the delivery DMZ.
uncertainty_note: PA06.08 is plausible where delivery environments should contain only a minimized subset, but the prompt does not explicitly state the governing scope constraints.

title: DMZ staging of data exceeds authorized delivery scope
description: The destination datastore may process or retain research data outside the bounds established for the delivery action, such as including extra subjects, attributes, or datasets not covered by the applicable authorization or purpose limitation. This undermines compliance with governing constraints on the delivery operation.
assumptions: Assumes the delivery process is bounded by explicit scope constraints such as data-sharing agreements, ethics approvals, or purpose limitation rules.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort mapping: PA06.08 clearly aligns to out-of-scope data use, but the exact LINDDUN Pro tree node for non-compliance may vary by catalog version.

title: Physical sample request discloses intent to obtain a biological specimen
description: By submitting a request for a physical sample from the DNA Store, the researcher reveals that a biological specimen associated with a person exists and is being sought for downstream sequencing. Even if the request contains only identifiers or case references, the act of requesting the specimen can disclose sensitive personal data about the subject's inclusion in a genomic workflow.
assumptions: Assumes the request references a specific sample, subject, or case in a way that can be tied to an identifiable or singled-out individual.
uncertainty_note: PA03.11 is an approximate grounding because this flow is a request for release of an already-collected biological sample, not the initial collection event itself.

title: DNA Store can use the request to re-identify or confirm the subject behind the sample
description: Upon receiving the sample request, the DNA Store may correlate request details, specimen identifiers, and internal records to re-associate the biological sample with a specific individual. This creates an identification threat if the request or store operations enable confirmation of the subject's identity beyond what is necessary to fulfill the transfer.
assumptions: Assumes the DNA Store maintains mappings between specimen identifiers and real-world identities or can access such mappings.
uncertainty_note: The PANOPTIC match is plausible where coded or pseudonymous sample identifiers are resolved by the store; if the sample is already fully identified for authorized handling, this may be less of a distinct threat.

title: Sample-request metadata can link researcher activity to a specific individual's genomic specimen
description: Metadata in the request flow—such as sample IDs, project references, timestamps, lab routing, or requester identity—can enable linkage between the researcher, the requested specimen, and the underlying data subject. This can expose participation in a study or treatment context even without transmitting the specimen itself.
assumptions: Assumes the request message carries persistent identifiers or contextual metadata observable in transit or logs.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 is used approximately here to ground the creation/transmission of a request artifact that represents the subject or specimen; a more exact PANOPTIC sub-activity for internal disclosure/transfer may exist outside the retrieved context.

title: Disclosure through release of a biological sample from the DNA Store
description: The DNA Store's act of handing over a physical biological sample to the NCCoE Researcher exposes highly sensitive genetic material. A biological sample can reveal extensive personal and familial information beyond the immediate research purpose, so the disclosure risk arises at the source when the sample is released.
assumptions: Assumes the physical sample is linked, or linkable, to an identifiable individual and is not fully anonymized in practice.
uncertainty_note: PA03.11 is defined around collection of biological materials from the data subject; here it is applied by analogy to downstream handling/release of that same biological sample because PANOPTIC treats privacy threats as action patterns around the artifact.

title: Detectability of a data subject via possession and inspection of the biological sample
description: Once the NCCoE Researcher retrieves the physical sample, the sample itself may make the data subject detectable or singled out through labels, accession identifiers, chain-of-custody markings, or intrinsic uniqueness of the specimen. Receipt and handling at the destination therefore create a detectability threat.
assumptions: Assumes the sample container or associated handling context includes identifiers or quasi-identifiers, or that the specimen is unique enough to support singling out.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort because the exact LINDDUN Pro detectability subtree available for this model was not provided.

title: Linkability from transfer metadata associated with sample retrieval
description: The act of transferring a physical sample from the DNA Store to a specific researcher can generate metadata such as request references, timestamps, custody logs, storage location, and researcher/sample associations. Even if the sample content is not directly examined in transit, this metadata can link the sample to a particular subject, study, or prior request.
assumptions: Assumes retrieval is logged or otherwise observable through inventory, custody, or transport records.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 Recording is used as the closest PANOPTIC fit for creation/use of retrieval records and artifacts around the transfer, not because the flow is literally audiovisual recording.

title: Physical sample transfer enables collection of a subject-representing artifact
description: By sending the physical sample to the sequencing lab, the researcher causes collection of a physical artifact that directly represents the data subject and can be used to derive context-relevant research data. This creates a detectability/privacy exposure risk because possession of the sample makes the subject materially observable to the recipient.
assumptions: Assumes the sample is human-derived or otherwise attributable to an individual data subject and is not fully anonymized before transfer.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC PA03.09 (Recording) is the closest retrieved sub-activity and appears applicable to capturing/holding a physical artifact, but the exact PANOPTIC fit for biospecimen handoff may be approximate.

title: Receiving clerk may collect sample beyond authorized scope
description: On receipt, the sequencing lab's intake function may collect or accept a physical sample whose collection falls outside the limits established by consent, protocol, ethics approval, or other governing rules. If the sample is accepted despite those limits, the flow contributes to disclosure or misuse through out-of-scope collection.
assumptions: Assumes there are scope boundaries from consent, IRB/protocol, contract, or policy that may restrict which samples may be accepted.
uncertainty_note: The retrieved context includes PA06.09.01, which is plausible for intake/acceptance of a sample, but the exact PANOPTIC mapping for a receiving clerk's role is somewhat approximate.

title: Receiving clerk may process sample outside governing constraints
description: After receipt, the sample may be logged, routed, labeled, or otherwise processed in ways that exceed the limits established by consent, protocol, or policy. Such out-of-scope handling undermines compliance and can enable downstream privacy harms.
assumptions: Assumes intake handling activities such as accessioning, labeling, and routing count as processing and are bounded by governance requirements.
uncertainty_note: PA06.09.02 was retrieved and is a reasonable fit for post-receipt intake handling, though the exact threat-tree node is best-effort due to limited PANOPTIC-to-LINDDUN mapping detail.

title: Request form records sensitive health context about the patient
description: By handing the patient a physical test request form, the clinician creates and discloses a tangible artifact that can represent sensitive aspects of the patient's health status, suspected condition, or intended genomic testing. If the form is seen, copied, or retained by unintended parties, the patient's personal data may be disclosed.
assumptions: Assumes the request form contains patient identifiers and/or clinical details related to the requested sample or sequencing test.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 is a best-fit PANOPTIC citation because the flow centers on provision of a physical artifact; the exact PANOPTIC sub-activity for issuing a requisition form may differ.

title: Sample request initiates collection of a biological specimen
description: The clinician's act of giving the patient the sample request form directly triggers collection of a biological sample from the patient for sequencing. Biological specimens are highly sensitive and can expose health, genetic, and familial information beyond the immediate testing purpose, creating a privacy threat if collection is excessive, insufficiently bounded, or poorly safeguarded downstream.
assumptions: Assumes the form is specifically for obtaining a biological sample that will be sent to a sequencing laboratory.
uncertainty_note: The privacy risk is grounded in the collection activity initiated by this flow rather than the paper handoff alone.

title: Biological sample request can enable linkage of patient identity to future specimen and genomic data
description: The request form likely carries identifiers or case details that accompany or are associated with the future specimen. This can enable linkage between the patient, the collected sample, and later sequencing results across clinical and laboratory contexts, increasing the risk that data from different stages of care are connected.
assumptions: Assumes the request form includes identifiers or reference numbers reused during sample collection and laboratory processing.
uncertainty_note: This linkage risk may materialize across subsequent handling steps, but the clinician's issuance of the request form is the initiating act.

title: Collection of a biological specimen from the patient
description: This flow represents the clinician obtaining a physical sample from the patient. The privacy threat arises at the source because the patient's biological material is being collected, exposing sensitive health information inherent in the specimen.
assumptions: Assumes the sample is newly obtained from the patient during this interaction, rather than merely handed over from prior storage.
uncertainty_note: The flow text says the clinician 'retrieves the physical sample referenced by the physical sample request', which could also mean pickup of an already-collected specimen. If so, PA03.11 is only approximate.

title: Processing and use of the received biological specimen by the clinician
description: Once the clinician receives the patient's physical sample, the specimen can reveal highly sensitive personal and health information through inspection, testing, or onward handling. The privacy threat arises at the destination because the recipient's subsequent use of the specimen may exceed the patient's expectations or the minimum necessary purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the clinician or associated care workflow will inspect, test, store, or otherwise use the specimen after receipt.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC PA03.11 clearly fits collection of biological material; mapping the downstream recipient-side privacy risk to Dd and tree node Dd.1 is best-effort because the exact subsequent processing is not described.

title: Collection of a physical specimen creates an identifying/representative artifact
description: By sending the physical sample onward for sequencing, the clinician causes collection/recording of a physical artifact that directly represents the patient and can later yield highly identifying genomic data. The privacy threat arises at the source because the act of sharing the specimen enables downstream identification and disclosure risks tied to the sample itself.
assumptions: The physical sample is patient-derived and traceable to an individual, directly or via accompanying labels/chain-of-custody information.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 'Recording' is the closest retrieved PANOPTIC activity because the specimen is a captured physical artifact; exact PANOPTIC wording may fit biospecimen collection only approximately.

title: Receiving and retaining the specimen beyond authorized scope
description: When the receiving clerk/lab accepts the physical sample, a privacy threat exists if collection/handling of the specimen exceeds the bounds authorized by consent, protocol, or governance (for example, retaining extra material, accepting a sample not needed for the stated research purpose, or routing it into broader uses). This is a destination-side threat because it depends on how the recipient receives and manages the specimen.
assumptions: The sequencing lab is expected to handle the sample only within a defined research, consent, and governance scope.
uncertainty_note: The retrieved PANOPTIC item PA06.09 is applicable if scope limits exist and could be exceeded; if the lab strictly follows protocol, this threat may not materialize on this flow.

title: Use of the specimen without valid consent or other governing basis
description: Acceptance and processing preparation of the physical sample can violate privacy expectations if the specimen is collected or handled outside the consent, notice, ethics approval, or other governing basis that bounds this transfer. The threat arises at the destination because the recipient's intake and subsequent handling determine whether the transfer remains within permitted scope.
assumptions: There are explicit consent, IRB/protocol, contractual, or policy constraints governing specimen transfer to the sequencing lab.
uncertainty_note: Mapped via PA06.09 because out-of-scope collection/handling commonly overlaps non-compliance; exact PANOPTIC-to-tree-node alignment is best-effort.

title: Requested digital sample data may enable re-identification
description: When the Digital Sample Data Store receives and fulfills the researcher's request, the selected digital sample data may contain direct identifiers, quasi-identifiers, or rich genomic/sample-linked attributes that allow a person to be re-identified, especially if the data will later be shared onward to a sequencing lab.
assumptions: Assumes the requested digital sample data relates to individuals and is not fully anonymous; genomic or sample-associated data is often inherently identifying or linkable.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC match PA05.01.01 is a best-fit based on the request/fulfillment of digital sample data; the flow description does not specify the exact fields returned.

title: Fulfilling the request discloses recorded digital artifacts about individuals
description: The Digital Sample Data Store processes a request for digital sample data that represents recorded artifacts about data subjects. Providing access to those records to the researcher increases disclosure risk because sensitive sample-derived information becomes available beyond its original point of collection.
assumptions: Assumes the digital sample data includes recorded digital representations or measurements tied to a person or specimen.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 Recording is relevant if the digital sample data consists of captured digital artifacts or measurements; if the store only returns non-personal operational metadata, this threat may not apply.

title: The request itself may create linkability between researcher, sample, and downstream sequencing activity
description: Metadata in the Digital Sample Data Request can link a particular researcher, requested sample set, and intended sequencing-lab transfer. Even if payload data is limited, the flow may reveal associations between records, projects, or individuals across systems and parties.
assumptions: Assumes the request contains sample identifiers, project identifiers, case references, or other metadata that can be correlated across systems.
uncertainty_note: Using PA05.01.01 here is approximate: the threat is primarily linkability from request metadata rather than explicit re-identification, but PANOPTIC retrieval suggests identification-related activity is relevant.

title: Researcher retrieval enables recording/copying of digital sample data
description: When the NCCoE Researcher retrieves digital sample data from the Digital Sample Data Store, the act of receipt can create a new copy or local representation of the sample data under the researcher's control. This constitutes a recording/capture of a digital artifact and increases the risk that the subject's data is disclosed beyond the original repository context.
assumptions: Assumes the retrieval results in a local copy, cached copy, export, or other researcher-accessible representation rather than only transient, tightly controlled in-place viewing.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC match PA03.09 (Recording) is a best-fit based on retrieval creating a researcher-held digital artifact; exact PANOPTIC sub-activity for access/retrieval may differ.

title: Retrieved sample data may enable implicit identification by the researcher
description: Once the NCCoE Researcher receives the digital sample data, combinations of attributes within the dataset may allow the researcher to infer or single out the data subject's identity, even if direct identifiers were limited in the request context. The privacy threat arises at the destination because identification is enabled by the recipient's analysis of the received data.
assumptions: Assumes the digital sample data contains quasi-identifiers, rare characteristics, or sufficient contextual detail to support re-identification or singling out.
uncertainty_note: The retrieved context lists PA05.01 as implicit identification; mapping to LINDDUN disclosure/identifiability is best-effort because PANOPTIC-to-tree-node alignment is approximate here.

title: Transfer metadata may link researcher access to a specific sample or subject
description: Even if the payload is protected, the retrieval flow itself can expose metadata such as which researcher accessed which digital sample, when, and how often. This can enable linkage between the researcher, the requested sample, and potentially the underlying data subject or case, revealing relationship patterns through the flow.
assumptions: Assumes network, application, or audit metadata about the retrieval is observable or retained and can be correlated with sample identifiers or request records.
uncertainty_note: PA05.01 is used as an approximate fit for inference/linkage from correlated metadata; a more precise PANOPTIC activity may exist outside the retrieved context.

title: Biological sample disclosure through transfer to research staff
description: The receiving clerk's act of sending a physical biological sample to the lab technician discloses highly sensitive specimen data to another party involved in the research workflow. The sample itself may reveal health, genetic, or other intimate characteristics of the data subject beyond what is strictly necessary for the immediate handling step.
assumptions: Assumes the physical sample is a biological specimen tied, directly or indirectly, to an identifiable or reasonably linkable individual.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC PA03.11 is a strong fit because the flow concerns a physical sample, but the exact LINDDUN tree node is best-effort because only the flow description is provided.

title: Linkability of specimen to subject or project at receipt
description: When the lab technician receives the physical sample, labels, handling context, or accompanying identifiers may allow the specimen to be linked to the same data subject across research activities or to other records associated with the project. This creates a privacy threat if the recipient can correlate the sample with additional datasets or prior samples.
assumptions: Assumes the sample carries identifiers, coded labels, or contextual metadata sufficient for correlation.
uncertainty_note: Linkability depends on whether the sample is coded, pseudonymized, or fully de-identified; this is not stated in the flow description.

title: Collection of sample beyond authorized research scope
description: Receipt of the physical sample by the lab technician may constitute collection for a research use that exceeds the scope authorized by consent, protocol, or governance constraints. If the technician's project access is broader than permitted, the transfer enables processing of specimen material outside approved bounds.
assumptions: Assumes there are purpose, consent, IRB, or role-based restrictions governing which projects or technicians may receive the sample.
uncertainty_note: This threat is conditional on governance limits not visible in the DFD; PA06.09 is included because out-of-scope collection is a plausible privacy risk for specimen transfers.

title: Creation of additional recorded artifacts from the sample
description: Upon receipt, the lab technician may create new recorded artifacts from the physical sample, such as images, assay outputs, extracted identifiers, or derivative records. These recordings can expand the amount of personal data held and increase downstream disclosure risk beyond the original transfer.
assumptions: Assumes normal lab handling includes documenting, imaging, or otherwise recording aspects of the sample.
uncertainty_note: PA03.09 is applied as a likely downstream action at the destination rather than something explicit in the flow itself.

title: Disclosure risk from transferring a biological sample to the wet lab
description: Sending a physical biological sample to the wet lab exposes highly sensitive specimen material that can reveal health, genetic, or other intimate attributes of the data subject beyond the immediate operational need. The privacy threat arises from the source's act of sharing the specimen with another processing context.
assumptions: Assumes the physical sample is a human biological specimen linked, or linkable, to an identifiable individual and is intended for sequencing.
uncertainty_note: PANOPTIC PA03.11 clearly fits biological specimen handling, but the exact LINDDUN tree-node mapping is best-effort because PANOPTIC is being used instead of the standard LINDDUN DFD-position methodology.

title: Detectability of the data subject through receipt and handling of the biological sample
description: Once the wet lab receives the physical sample for sequencing, the mere presence and handling of that specimen can make the data subject detectable as someone undergoing laboratory analysis or genomic processing, even before sequencing results are produced.
assumptions: Assumes sample custody, labeling, or intake procedures allow the specimen to be associated with a particular person or case.
uncertainty_note: This is a plausible PANOPTIC-grounded detectability threat from biological sample intake, but the detectability characterization depends on how samples are labeled and segregated in practice.

title: Linkability via sample transfer metadata and chain-of-custody information
description: The transfer of the physical sample may generate shipment, accessioning, or chain-of-custody metadata that can link the specimen to the same individual across collection, transport, and sequencing stages. Even if direct identifiers are minimized, consistent sample identifiers or contextual metadata can enable correlation.
assumptions: Assumes the transfer uses labels, case numbers, timestamps, courier records, or other persistent metadata.
uncertainty_note: The PANOPTIC grounding is indirect here: PA03.11 covers biological sample collection/handling, while the linkability risk specifically stems from transfer metadata rather than the specimen alone.

title: Insufficient explanation of downstream handling of shared results copy
description: When the Genetic Counselor provides the Patient with a copy of interpreted clinical results and recommendations, the sharing may omit clear communication about how that copy should be handled, stored, or further disclosed to other parties (e.g., family members, employers, insurers, other clinicians). This can leave the patient without enough context to judge downstream disclosure risks and stewardship responsibilities associated with highly sensitive genetic information.
assumptions: Applies if the counselor provides the results copy or recommendations without adequately explaining foreseeable downstream privacy implications or responsibilities tied to onward sharing.
uncertainty_note: PA06.06 is framed around downstream stewardship responsibilities and is only a partial fit here because the recipient is the data subject rather than a conventional downstream custodian.

title: Patient may receive results in a form that limits practical control over their information
description: If the Patient is given the interpreted clinical results only in a constrained format or channel, they may be unable to effectively manage the content afterward, such as selectively copying, moving, editing, or storing it in a privacy-preserving way. This reduces the individual's practical control over their own sensitive genetic information.
assumptions: Applies if the copy of results is delivered in a locked portal, non-exportable format, or otherwise constrained medium.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on the delivery format of the copy; the flow description does not specify whether the patient's ability to manage the information is actually restricted.

title: Consultation or result-sharing interaction may be recorded
description: The meeting in which the Genetic Counselor reviews results and provides recommendations may be audio-, video-, screen-, or document-recorded, creating an additional artifact of the patient's sensitive genetic information and counseling discussion. Such recording increases the amount of personal data captured and may expose highly sensitive health and hereditary information beyond what is necessary for the immediate consultation.
assumptions: Applies if the consultation, telehealth session, screen display, or transmitted copy of results is recorded by either party or by supporting systems.
uncertainty_note: The retrieved PANOPTIC activity PA03.09 is relevant, but the flow description does not explicitly state that recording occurs; this is a plausible threat pattern rather than a confirmed behavior.

title: Patient may lack meaningful control over onward disclosure of interpreted genetic results
description: When the Genetic Physician communicates interpreted clinical genetic results and recommendations to the patient, the disclosure may occur without giving the patient granular control over what specific findings are shared, how much detail is included, or whether particularly sensitive incidental or familial implications are deferred. This can undermine the patient's ability to control disclosure of highly sensitive genetic information.
assumptions: Assumes the communication channel or clinical workflow does not support patient choice about scope/timing/detail of disclosure, or that disclosure is effectively mandatory once results are available.
uncertainty_note: PA07.04 is the closest PANOPTIC match from the provided context, but applicability depends on whether the patient truly lacks choice in this disclosure workflow.

title: Interpreted genetic results could be intercepted in transit to the patient
description: The flow carries sensitive interpreted clinical genetic results and professional recommendations from the physician to the patient. If transmitted over insecure channels or exposed during delivery, an unauthorized party could observe the contents, revealing health status, genetic traits, or familial implications.
assumptions: Assumes the results may be delivered through a channel with interception risk, such as unsecured email, portal misconfiguration, paper mail exposure, or overheard verbal communication.
uncertainty_note: High confidence that interception is a relevant generic in-transit privacy threat; exact PANOPTIC citation is based on the retrieved PA03.07 context.

title: Clinical report generation processes research data beyond authorized scope
description: The Clinical Result Generation App may use context-relevant research data for creating a final clinical report in ways that exceed the limits established for the original research-data use, such as repurposing research-only attributes for clinical decision support or report content without an appropriate legal, ethical, or governance basis. This creates a disclosure/use threat because the destination processes data outside the permitted scope on receipt.
assumptions: Assumes the dataset in the cluster filesystem contains research-context data whose permitted uses may be narrower than direct clinical reporting, or that only a subset is approved for clinical-result generation.
uncertainty_note: The PANOPTIC citation is best-effort based on the retrieved context and the flow description; applicability depends on actual consent, governance approvals, and whether this research dataset is explicitly authorized for clinical reporting.

title: Cluster filesystem shares data types that are out of scope for clinical report generation
description: The Cluster Filesystem may disclose context-relevant research data that includes fields, records, or data categories not necessary or permitted for the Clinical Result Generation App's reporting purpose. Sending out-of-scope data from the source increases the risk that unnecessary sensitive research information is incorporated into downstream clinical workflows.
assumptions: Assumes the source store may contain broader research data than is strictly needed to create the final clinical report.
uncertainty_note: This threat applies if the source does not adequately constrain which data types are exported on GF18; the flow description alone does not prove over-sharing.

title: Clinical result generation bypasses privacy or governance controls on research data
description: The Clinical Result Generation App could circumvent or ignore privacy controls attached to research data in the cluster filesystem, such as purpose restrictions, access gating, de-identification requirements, or workflow checks, and proceed to generate a clinical report anyway. This undermines users' or governance bodies' ability to control how the data is used.
assumptions: Assumes privacy or governance controls exist for the research data and that the destination app has a technical path to receive or use the data without fully enforcing them.
